parole.significato: A salutation, especially a drinking toast.
parole.testo: From Chinese Pidgin English chin-chin, a reduplication of Shanghainese 請 /请 (⁵chin, “please”). Sometimes, especially in Italianate spellings, reborrowed from Italian cincin.

parole.significato: A Chinese person, or person of Chinese descent.
parole.testo: From Chinese Pidgin English. Calque of Chinese 中國人 /中国人 (Zhōngguórén) ("China + -man"). Applied also to ships by analogy with East Indiaman.

parole.significato: Used to urge someone to do something quickly.
parole.testo: From Chinese Pidgin English, from Cantonese 速速 (cuk1 cuk1, “quick”). Recorded in English since the 1830s (see citations for adverb). Recorded as a Chinese term in 1795.

The term was earliest applied to fishing tackle (from 1615), later being transferred to the dining utensil (attested since 1637) driven by their visual resemblance. Shortened from chow-chow, from Chinese Pidgin English chow-chow. Compare Macanese chau-cháu. See also English chow fun, chow mein, etc.
Borrowed from Chinese Pidgin English chow-chow (“food”). Compare Macanese chau-cháu.

parole.significato: A Chinese household divinity; a Chinese idol.
parole.testo: From Chinese Pidgin English joss, from Macau Pidgin Portuguese, from Portuguese deus (“god”), from Latin deus (“god”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god/that which belongs to heaven”). Doublet of Tiw and Tyr.
Attributed to various forms of pidgin English, most prominently from Chinese Pidgin English.

parole.significato: A brief examination, a peek or glance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinese Pidgin English look-see.
From Chinese Pidgin English, calquing Chinese 不能做 (bùnéng zuò, “cannot do”).
